clue.text: see 22dn.
Old leader from old city with pecker in an erect state

indicators.note: in a down clue, standing something upright means reading it from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: Ur of the Chaldees, the crossword's favourite ancient city
a hen pecks at its grain, so it is a pecker

explanation.surface: A smutty image of an ancient ruler from a lost city, sexually aroused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pecker' and 'erect' push the Private Eye reader towards smut; the pecker is only a hen, and 'erect' is the down-clue signal to read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Jawaharlal Nehru was India's first prime minister after independence, a national head of government from decades past.

clue.text: Jock about right, er, as a nut case?

indicators.note: about in its sense of around, so a piece is surrounded by another

parts.note: Jock is a nickname for a Scotsman
the standard abbreviation for right
both are sounds of hesitation

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a hesitant Scotsman is mad.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'nut case' looks like a lunatic; read literally it is the case that holds the nuts, slang for testicles, and the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Testicles are called nuts in slang, and this pouch of skin is the container that holds them.

clue.text: Poet: "Dolby is free — O, could it be?"

indicators.note: letters set free are no longer held in their order, so they can be rearranged

parts.note: taken as it stands, as anagram fodder
taken as it stands, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A poet quoted as musing hopefully about Dolby sound becoming free.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon makes 'Poet' look like the definition with a quotation to follow; in fact it is fodder, and the definition is the wistful 'O, could it be?' at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Group O is one of the human blood groups, so O is an example of the thing named.

clue.text: Complaint when useless Mandelson starts entering a blog (crappy)

indicators.note: whatever enters goes inside something else, so one piece sits within another
something crappy is badly made, so its letters are in poor order and need rearranging

parts.note: taken as it stands, as anagram fodder

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, so only the first of each is kept

parts.note: the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Someone moans that Peter Mandelson, the Labour minister, has joined the blogosphere, and badly.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter Mandelson was a senior Labour politician in 2009; the moan in the surface is really the definition, a medical complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint in the medical sense is an ailment, and this painful lower back condition is one such ailment.

clue.text: see 8dn.
News delivered by stupid gits covering row

indicators.note: to cover something is to wrap around it, so one piece encloses another
a stupid arrangement is a senseless one, so the letters must be put in another order

parts.note: taken as it stands, as anagram fodder
a row is a loud noise, a din

explanation.surface: A jibe that the news is brought to us by idiots squabbling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' is the noise sense (rhymes with cow), not a line; a git is British slang for a contemptible person.
explanation.definitionFit: Tidings is an old-fashioned word for information or reports, which is what news means.

clue.text: (& 6dn.) Quickly putting away spliff, go in, oh so dopey

indicators.note: dopey means befuddled, as if drugged, so the letters come out in a confused order

parts.note: taken as it stands, as anagram fodder, twelve letters

explanation.surface: Someone stoned, rushing to finish a joint while muttering vaguely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting away spliff' reads as stubbing out a joint, but 'putting away' belongs with 'Quickly' as the definition; a spliff is a cannabis cigarette.
explanation.definitionFit: To put food away is to eat it, and finishing a meal rapidly is described with this idiom.

clue.text: Failure to vote Lab (leader lacking, so intent on "spinning")

indicators.note: without its leader a word loses its first letter

parts.note: Lab, short for Labour, without its first letter

indicators.note: spinning things round jumbles their order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as it stands, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A dig at Labour: with no leader worth the name, it is obsessed with spin, so voters stay home.
explanation.walkthrough: In 2009 Labour was mocked for spin, meaning media manipulation; here spinning is only the signal to shuffle letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal decision not to cast a ballot, either for or against, is exactly what this word names.

clue.text: Blair (not that is, one shielded by bum crazy fat kid)

definitions.note: the answer is plural (cherubs), the definition singular

indicators.note: 'not' tells us to take away the letters that 'that is' stands for

parts.note: Cherie Blair, wife of Tony Blair, the Prime Minister
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

indicators.note: something shielded is surrounded by its protector, so one piece goes inside
crazy means disordered, so the letters around it are scrambled

parts.note: taken as it stands, as anagram fodder
the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A playground insult, with 'Blair' in brackets as if pointing out which Blair is meant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blair' pulls towards Tony; it is Cherie who loses 'ie'. The brackets try to make the aside look like commentary rather than wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Cherubs are painted as chubby winged infants, so plump children are loosely what these angels look like.

clue.text: Doctor Death's first day entered in dossier

indicators.note: what is entered in something is put inside it, so these pieces sit within another

parts.note: a dossier is a file of documents

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
the standard abbreviation for day

explanation.surface: A police dossier on 'Doctor Death', the tabloid name for the serial killer Harold Shipman, gains a date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor Death' reads as one name; split it, and 'Doctor' is a verb meaning tamper with.
explanation.definitionFit: To doctor accounts or evidence is to falsify them, and to cook the books dishonestly in this way is the verb meant.

clue.text: Pair of tits, ones replaced with uranium implants, shouldn't be allowed

indicators.note: to replace is to put new letters where the old stood while the rest keeps its place

parts.note: two of the small birds, one after the other
the Roman numeral one, twice over
U is the chemical symbol for uranium, used for each swap
surface padding: the uranium is what gets put in, like an implant

explanation.surface: A disapproving remark about breast implants.
explanation.walkthrough: The tits are birds, not breasts, and 'implants' is surface dressing for the uranium going in where each I was.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the clicking exclamation people make to express disapproval, much as saying something ought to be banned.

clue.text: Bum, almost round isn't wobbling — flaming criminal

indicators.note: almost all of a word means dropping its final letter

parts.note: arse, British slang for a bottom, without its last letter

indicators.note: something wobbling is unsteady and out of place, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: O is round in shape
taken as it stands, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An insult hurled at a crook: his backside is not quite wobbly, and he is a flaming criminal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flaming' reads as the mild British swear word; here it is literal, a criminal who sets fires.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who deliberately sets property on fire commits a crime, so the fire-raising offender is literally a criminal with flames.

clue.text: Figures leader of Tories is implicated in something shocking with Sun

indicators.note: being implicated means being caught up inside, so a piece sits within another

parts.note: static electricity gives you a shock

indicators.note: a leader comes first, so only the opening letter of the word is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
taken as it stands
S is the abbreviation for Sunday, and also for sun

explanation.surface: Figures show the Conservative leader mixed up in a scandal with The Sun newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid that switched to backing the Tories in 2009; 'shocking' is literal, the jolt that static gives.
explanation.definitionFit: Statistics are numerical data, which is what 'figures' means when people quote numbers in a report.

clue.text: Skip, a non-moral bastard, perpetrator of minor violation

indicators.note: used as a coarse intensifier, it marks the preceding words as corrupted and out of order

parts.note: taken as it stands, as anagram fodder, thirteen letters

explanation.surface: An amoral skipper denounced as a bastard, but only for a petty offence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minor violation' sounds like a small offence; the film director had pleaded guilty in 1977 to unlawful sex with a 13-year-old, a minor, and was arrested in Switzerland in 2009.
explanation.definitionFit: The film director fled America before sentencing for sexual abuse of an underage girl, so he committed a crime against a child.

clue.text: Toss sailor (declared gay) and laugh uncontrollably?

parts.note: to toss dice is to roll them
AB, able-bodied seaman
someone openly gay has come out

explanation.surface: Someone mocks a sailor who has just come out, finding it hilarious.
explanation.walkthrough: The brackets make 'declared gay' look like an aside about the sailor; it is a piece of the wordplay in its own right.
explanation.definitionFit: People helpless with mirth are said to be rolling in the aisles, tumbling around with hilarity.

clue.text: One who fusses about Brenda, maybe, Sarah Palin?

definitions.text: One who fusses about Brenda, maybe
definitions.meaning: Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, and a royal attendant fusses around her
read literally, a woman waiting in the wings for the top job

explanation.surface: Sarah Palin pictured as a fussing attendant to someone named Brenda.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye has long called the Queen 'Brenda'. Palin, the 2008 Republican vice-presidential candidate, was widely expected to run for president, so she was waiting in the wings.
explanation.definitionFit: A noblewoman who attends a queen at court fusses around her, and the phrase read literally describes a woman awaiting her turn at power.

clue.text: see 20ac.
Cyclops has grief from females, endlessly, holding the centre of their lives

indicators.note: without an end a word loses its last letter
to hold something is to have it inside you, so pieces go within another

parts.note: women, without the final letter

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the middle letter of this five-letter word
something that lives exists, it is

explanation.surface: The setter complains of the misery women cause him, even while they are the centre of men's lives.
explanation.walkthrough: Cyclops is the setter's pseudonym, so the definition is the setter lamenting in the first person.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation is a traditional first-person lament, so it is what the setter would say when full of sorrow.

clue.text: One politician for everyone to charge with treason?

parts.note: the Roman numeral one
Member of Parliament
each and everyone are close in sense

explanation.surface: A demand that every politician be tried for betraying the nation.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that treason is only one of the offences this procedure covers.
explanation.definitionFit: Formally accusing a public official of serious misconduct, historically including betraying the state, is the legislative procedure meant.

clue.text: (& 17dn.) Novelist's dirty underwear cellar — not one on left

indicators.note: something dirty is in a mess, so these letters are jumbled
'not' drops a letter and 'on' puts another in its place, so one letter is exchanged

parts.note: taken as it stands, as anagram fodder, fifteen letters
a, the indefinite article, means one
the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: The possessive suggests a novelist's soiled underwear kept in a cellar.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the two As in the fodder is swapped for an L before the letters are rearranged. The possessive in 'Novelist's' means 'is' joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The British writer is best known for The Alexandria Quartet, a sequence of four novels set in Egypt.

clue.text: Word processor gets Truss annoyed over the radio

indicators.note: on the radio we only hear words, so the spelling may differ

parts.note: to truss is to tie up, and pissed off means annoyed

explanation.surface: Lynne Truss, the grammar stickler who wrote Eats, Shoots and Leaves, gets irritated by a writer's work on air.
explanation.walkthrough: Truss looks like the author, whose surname tempts you toward punctuation; it is the verb, meaning tie up.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who enters text on a keyboard handles words, so the office clerk is a human processor of them.

clue.text: (& 1ac.) Shock condition of teararses when separated

indicators.note: separating the compound word into its two parts lets each part be clued alone

parts.note: the first half of the run-together word: to tear is to rip apart
the second half: British slang for backsides

explanation.surface: The state of shock of reckless drivers ('tearaways') when they are split up.
explanation.walkthrough: A shock here is a mass of hair, not a fright; 'teararses' is a Private Eye blend of tearaway and arse.
explanation.definitionFit: Damaged hair whose strands fray at the tips is a hair problem, and a shock is a thick head of hair.

clue.text: Jolly's after orifice — hide!

indicators.note: 'after' fixes the order, so the first piece named comes second

parts.note: an orifice is an opening
someone feeling up is cheerful

explanation.surface: A lewd warning to hide once someone jolly is after your orifice.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', setting the jolly piece after the other one.
explanation.definitionFit: To go to ground and shelter out of sight somewhere is the phrasal verb, an imperative matching the exclamation.

clue.text: (& 27ac.) Head eating the rolled bogey

indicators.note: rolling letters moves them round the end in a loop, keeping their order
what is eaten goes inside the eater, so one piece swallows another

parts.note: the pate is the top of the head
the word's letters rolled round until the E leads

explanation.surface: Someone eating a rolled-up bogey, dried snot, from their nose.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes a bogey nasal; it is the bogeyman sense, a thing one dreads or loathes.
explanation.definitionFit: A bogey, like a bugbear, is something that causes particular annoyance or dread, a personal peeve.

clue.text: "Matey" Blair's pissed with Coe — not right

indicators.note: 'not' removes the letter that 'right' stands for
pissed is British slang for drunk, and drunk letters stagger into a new order

parts.note: taken as it stands, with the R removed
Sebastian Coe, the athlete and Tory peer, taken as it stands

explanation.surface: Tony Blair, drunk with Sebastian Coe (who ran London's Olympic bid), is being 'matey'.
explanation.walkthrough: Only one R goes, the one in Blair; the quotation marks around 'Matey' mock Blair's famous chumminess.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is friendly and enjoys company behaves like a mate, companionably and warmly toward others.

clue.text: University goes in for bondage, bounding one drunk, from which gas and water are taken?

definitions.text: from which gas and water are taken?

indicators.note: to bound something is to form its boundary, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: the standard abbreviation for university
ties are bonds
the Roman numeral one
lit is slang for drunk

explanation.surface: A university takes up bondage with a drunk tied up, and then people take its gas and water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes in for' reads as 'takes up a hobby'; it simply joins the U to the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Public services such as electricity, gas and water supply are the companies consumers draw these supplies from.

clue.text: see 24dn.
